newsitem.title: FRANCE: France rules out suit against far-rightist Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: France rules out suit against far-rightist Le Pen.

text.p: French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon on Thursday ruled out legal action against far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen over his espousal of racial inequality, but said loopholes in laws against racism should be closed.
Toubon said he would soon send to parliament a proposal to tighten the laws against spreading xenophobia and racism after Le Pen said that inequality between races was "a fact".

"The words in question do not appear to constitute a violation of the penal code or of press laws, as the principle of equality contained in the Declaration of Human Rights is not directly included in law," Toubon said in a statement.
Defence Minister Charles Millon said France should use all available legal weapons against the outspoken far-right leader.
"Can one say with impunity that human beings do not have equal rights and dignity?" Millon asked on RTL radio.
"If our current legal and judicial arsenal is inadequate, then parliament must take up this matter," he added.
Eric Raoult, junior minister for territorial planning, urban affairs and integration, said that Le Pen was "turning into a Nazi" while his National Front party "has become fascist".
Numerous human rights organisations and political leaders, most from the opposition Left, have advocated banning Le Pen's National Front or taking it to court.

Toubon said the legal requirements to ban the National Front were not met. His statement also meant that Le Pen's remarks were not covered by laws punishing inciting racial hatred by up to a year in prison, fines of up to 300,000 francs ($60,000) and five years' ineligibility for public office.
An unrepentant Le Pen said in a television interview on Wednesday, "I don't see why saying one does not believe in racial equality is a violation of human dignity.
"I will not be intimidated by the demonstrations or the threats of a "thought police'," he told LCI television.

The National Front sparked fresh controversy by planning a demonstration on Saturday in the southern port city Marseille after a 15-year-old youth of North African descent was arrested in the stabbing death of a white Marseille youth.
Even before the arrest, the Front denounced the crime as "a crime against France, committed by immigrant thugs of North African origin".
Both the murder victim's father and Marseille mayor Jean-Claude Gaudin criticised the politicisation of the crime.

The row over the National Front's role in French politics occurred amidst discussion of election law reforms expected to help the Front break into the National Assembly, where it now has no seats, in the 1998 general elections.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe had last week proposed a reform in election law that political analysts said would enable the Front to win a sizeable bloc of seats in the National Assembly.

A major goal of the reforms appeared to be an attempt at winning goodwill from Le Pen, who has routinely opposed all the ruling centre-right's candidates, even when a Front candidate was not in the race.

Le Pen, whose slogan is "France for the French" and who once dismissed Nazi gas chambers as "a mere detail in the history of World War Two", won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential elections.
